newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Little hope for Afghan peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Little hope for Afghan peace talks.

text.p: Attempts by the United Nations to persuade the warring factions in Afghanistan to settle their differences through negotiations suffered another setback on Saturday when the Taleban told the U.N. that they wanted the issue of an exchange of prisoners of war to be settled before talks start.

This is just the latest holdup in the long-running but so far ineffectual attempts of the U.N. and other international bodies to stop the internecine war that engulfed Afghanistan after the communist regime was deposed in 1992.

The history of attempts to bring the factions together is depressing. In 1993, an agreement to form a coalition government, signed in Mecca, Islam's holiest city, broke down after four days in a hail of rocket fire.
In 1995 the U.N. believed that it had an agreement in which the President would step down in favour of an interim government. That failed when the Taleban refused to be part of the agreement.
Since the Taleban took over Kabul last year, the U.N. has tried different approaches, with a similar lack of success.

It convened a meeting of countries that were believed to be able to exert an influence on the factions, but this produced little more than a statement that the participants believed that a military solution was not possible.
More recently the U.N. has convened "technical level discussions" between representatives of the belligerents in the Pakistani capital Islamabad.
They have produced little of substance. The Taleban demand for an exchange of prisoners of war was in response to a U.N. invitation to attend further discussions.

The numerous meetings that have taken place over the years between the antagonists have been marked by mistrust and unrealistic demands, and finally rendered meaningless by the rapidly changing military situation on the ground in Afghanistan.
While all the factions pay lip-service to their interest in a negotiated solution, at least one analyst in Kabul believes that talks are doomed to failure.

"The parties use talks as another tactic to forward their military ends. After all this time without any progress, it is difficult to believe that the leaders are really interested in a compromise solution." said the analyst, who wished to remain anonymous.

He says that in the past the parties have used the military hiatus that takes place during talks to rearm and redeploy their forces. "When one of the parties felt weak on the battlefield, it offered talks, but while the talks were going on it used the opportunity to reinforce its positions.

"It has happened so often that no one belives that an offer of talks is anything more than an attempt to gain a breathing space and gain a degree of international acceptability by being seen to cooperate with the U.N." he said.
Mullah Mohammed Omar, the leader of the Taleban, was quoted by the BBC as saying earlier this month that they had lost faith in a negotiated solution and would fight to the finish.
The intractability of the parties to the conflict in Afghanistan has left the U.N. on the sidelines.
Dr. Norbert Holl, the U.N. special envoy to Afghanistan, maintains that a military solution to the Afghan conflict is not possible.

"It is the position of the United Nations that a military solution to the Afghan problem is not possible. This is the clear policy of the United Nations whatever happens on the ground," said Holl on a recent visit to Kabul.
The Taleban are still elated by their capture of Kabul and firm in their belief that God and time are on their side. The opposition see no future for themselves in an Afghanistan run by the Taleban.
While these beliefs remain -- and there are few signs that they will change in the near future -- the prospects for a negotiated peace are remote.
